findings.title: Persistent storage write without TTL management
findings.description: A contract entry point writes to persistent storage but does not call `extend_ttl`, `set_ttl`, or `bump` in the same function or in the intra-file helpers it calls. Persistent entries have a time-to-live; if it is not extended, stored data can expire and be lost. TTL may legitimately be managed elsewhere (for example in a separate maintenance entry point), so this is a low-confidence signal.
findings.evidence: persistent storage write without TTL extension in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: When writing persistent data that must survive, extend its time-to-live with `storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...)` after the write. Prefer a single, well-documented TTL policy for the contract. If TTL is managed centrally, suppress this rule for the function.

findings.title: Privileged state change without an event
findings.description: A contract entry point mutates a storage key that looks like privileged configuration (for example admin, owner, pause, params, fees, or oracle) without publishing an event. Off-chain indexers and users rely on events to observe critical changes; without one, the change is invisible to monitoring and incident response.
findings.evidence: privileged storage change without an event in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: Publish an event with `env.events().publish(...)` for every privileged state change, including the old and new values where practical. Keep the event schema stable so indexers can rely on it.

findings.title: State-changing entry point without caller authorization
findings.description: A public contract function mutates storage but does not call require_auth or require_auth_for_args anywhere in its body or in the intra-file helper functions it calls. Without an authorization check, any account can invoke the function and change contract state, which may allow theft, privilege escalation, or corruption of contract data. This is a heuristic: authorization may legitimately be enforced by a callee or be intentionally absent for permissionless operations.
findings.evidence: `set` storage mutation with no authorization in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: Call `address.require_auth()` (or `require_auth_for_args`) for the account that must approve the operation before mutating state. Prefer authorizing a specific argument that binds the approval to the operation rather than authorizing a stored admin address unconditionally. If the function is intentionally permissionless, document that and suppress this rule for the function.

findings.title: Unchecked arithmetic in a contract entry point
findings.description: A public contract entry point performs binary arithmetic (`+`, `-`, or `*`) on values without a checked, saturating, overflowing, or wrapping operation. In release builds Rust arithmetic wraps on overflow and underflow instead of panicking, so a decrement below zero (or an overflow) can silently produce an incorrect result — a common cause of balance and accounting bugs in token, escrow and vault contracts. This is a heuristic: it cannot prove that the operands are attacker-influenced or that their range is constrained, so it reports low confidence and should be reviewed in context.
findings.evidence: unchecked `-` arithmetic in entry point `withdraw`: balance - amount (use `checked_sub` and handle `None`)
findings.remediation: Use explicit checked arithmetic (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`) and handle the `None` case with a typed contract error, or use saturating/overflowing variants when that semantics is intended. Prefer checked operations for balances, amounts, and counters derived from user input.

findings.title: Token transfer amount without validation
findings.description: A public contract entry point passes a caller-supplied amount to `transfer` or `transfer_from` without comparing it against zero. Token implementations differ in how they treat negative or out-of-range amounts; a missing guard can therefore move an unintended value, corrupt accounting, or revert in surprising ways. This is a heuristic: it cannot prove that the token rejects the value or that another layer validates it, so it reports low confidence.
findings.evidence: `transfer` transfers unchecked amount `amount` in entry point `payout`
findings.remediation: Validate the amount before transferring, for example reject `amount <= 0` with a typed contract error (or check both bounds when the token has a maximum). Validate once at the entry point and pass the checked value to `transfer`/`transfer_from`.

findings.description: A string literal in the contract matches the shape of a Stellar account (`G...`) or contract (`C...`) address. Hardcoding an address bakes a fixed counterparty or administrator into the contract, preventing rotation and making the contract unsafe if that key or contract changes or is compromised. findings.title: Unbounded storage iteration in an entry point
findings.description: A contract entry point iterates over storage. If the iterated collection grows without bound, the operation's resource cost grows with it and may exceed Soroban's ledger entry, CPU, or memory limits, causing the entry point to fail (a denial of service). Soroban does not provide storage enumeration in the same way as some platforms, so patterns that loop over persistent collections built by the contract are the usual cause.
findings.evidence: storage iteration in `count_all`: env . storage () . persistent () . keys ()
findings.remediation: Bound the amount of work performed per invocation: paginate with an explicit limit, maintain aggregate values instead of scanning, or cap the number of entries processed and return partial results. Ensure any loop over storage is bounded by a value the contract controls.

Persistent entries have a time-to-live; if it is not extended, stored data can expire and be lost. TTL may legitimately be managed elsewhere (for example in a separate maintenance entry point), so this is a low-confidence signal.
findings.evidence: persistent storage write without TTL extension in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: When writing persistent data that must survive, extend its time-to-live with `storage().persistent().extend_ttl(...)` after the write. Prefer a single, well-documented TTL policy for the contract. If TTL is managed centrally, suppress this rule for the function.

findings.title: Privileged state change without an event
findings.description: A contract entry point mutates a storage key that looks like privileged configuration (for example admin, owner, pause, params, fees, or oracle) without publishing an event. Off-chain indexers and users rely on events to observe critical changes; without one, the change is invisible to monitoring and incident response.
findings.evidence: privileged storage change without an event in `set_admin`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& symbol_short ! ("ADMIN") , & new_admin)
findings.remediation: Publish an event with `env.events().publish(...)` for every privileged state change, including the old and new values where practical. Keep the event schema stable so indexers can rely on it.

findings.title: Hardcoded Stellar account or contract address
findings.description: A string literal in the contract matches the shape of a Stellar account (`G...`) or contract (`C...`) address. Hardcoding an address bakes a fixed counterparty or administrator into the contract, preventing rotation and making the contract unsafe if that key or contract changes or is compromised. Addresses are public, so this is a design concern rather than a secret leak.
findings.evidence: hardcoded Stellar address literal: GAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA
findings.remediation: Store addresses in contract storage or pass them as parameters, and validate them against stored configuration. If an address must be a compile-time constant, document the operational plan for rotation and key compromise.

findings.title: Unchecked arithmetic in a contract entry point
findings.description: A public contract entry point performs binary arithmetic (`+`, `-`, or `*`) on values without a checked, saturating, overflowing, or wrapping operation. In release builds Rust arithmetic wraps on overflow and underflow instead of panicking, so a decrement below zero (or an overflow) can silently produce an incorrect result — a common cause of balance and accounting bugs in token, escrow and vault contracts. This is a heuristic: it cannot prove that the operands are attacker-influenced or that their range is constrained, so it reports low confidence and should be reviewed in context.
findings.evidence: unchecked `-` arithmetic in entry point `withdraw`: balance - amount (use `checked_sub` and handle `None`)
findings.remediation: Use explicit checked arithmetic (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`) and handle the `None` case with a typed contract error, or use saturating/overflowing variants when that semantics is intended. Prefer checked operations for balances, amounts, and counters derived from user input.

findings.title: Panic-prone construct in a contract entry point
findings.description: A contract entry point calls `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!`, `todo!`, `unimplemented!`, or `unreachable!`. In Soroban these abort the invocation and roll back state. When reachable from normal input, this turns a recoverable error condition into a failed transaction (a denial of service). This is a code-quality signal rather than proof of a vulnerability.
findings.evidence: `unwrap` in `close` can panic: env . storage () . persistent () . get (& DataKey :: Deadline) . unwrap ()
findings.remediation: Return a `Result` with a typed contract error instead of panicking, so callers can handle failure. Replace `unwrap`/`expect` on fallible operations with `?`, `unwrap_or`, `unwrap_or_default`, or explicit matching.

findings.title: State-changing entry point without caller authorization
findings.description: A public contract function mutates storage but does not call require_auth or require_auth_for_args anywhere in its body or in the intra-file helper functions it calls. Without an authorization check, any account can invoke the function and change contract state, which may allow theft, privilege escalation, or corruption of contract data. This is a heuristic: authorization may legitimately be enforced by a callee or be intentionally absent for permissionless operations.
findings.evidence: `set` storage mutation with no authorization in `close`: env . storage () . persistent () . set (& DataKey :: Closed , & true)
findings.remediation: Call `address.require_auth()` (or `require_auth_for_args`) for the account that must approve the operation before mutating state. Prefer authorizing a specific argument that binds the approval to the operation rather than authorizing a stored admin address unconditionally. If the function is intentionally permissionless, document that and suppress this rule for the function.

findings.title: Insecure randomness derived from ledger state
findings.description: A public contract entry point uses the ledger timestamp or ledger sequence in arithmetic, modulo, or a comparison that appears to select an outcome. Ledger values are publicly known and can be influenced by transaction submission timing, so deriving randomness from them is predictable and may let an attacker steer lotteries, winner selection, or other value-dependent logic. This is a heuristic: it reports low confidence and cannot prove that the value is used as randomness or that an attacker can control the result.
findings.evidence: ledger `timestamp` may be predictable and is used in an outcome-selecting modulo in entry point `draw`: env . ledger () . timestamp () % 100
findings.remediation: Do not derive randomness from `ledger().timestamp()` or `ledger().sequence()`. Use a commitment/reveal scheme, a verifiable randomness source, or another design that does not depend on ledger values the submitter can observe or influence. If the value is only used for an expiry check against a stored deadline, document the use and suppress this rule.
